title: A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
gist: The 417-page, technology-neutral Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) faces a Senate vote on November 9 and would narrow federal permitting and impose review deadlines for energy projects. Modeled outcomes diverge sharply: Rhodium and RFF see modest emission cuts and big cost savings, while a Purdue model finds emissions would have risen because easier permitting also unleashes data-center-driven natural-gas plants; the Democratic midterm wins add uncertainty over timing.

themes.theme: BAAJA bill design and political path

insights.claim: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a 417-page permitting reform bill, narrows which energy projects need federal permits and sets review deadlines to shorten approvals that can currently take years.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Faster permitting would compress development timelines and cost of capital for power plants, transmission and pipelines.

insights.claim: BAAJA is largely technology neutral, opening the door to both fossil-fuel and renewable buildout, which has produced an unusual coalition of supporters across parties and interest groups.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Both gas infrastructure and clean-energy developers stand to benefit, rather than a clear sector winner.
insights.quote: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables.

insights.claim: BAAJA has two Republican and two Democratic Senate sponsors and is backed by the White House, whose Council of Economic Advisors found it would reduce review times and boost GDP.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Executive support raises the odds of enactment in some form.
insights.locator: The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate

insights.claim: The Senate vote on BAAJA is set for November 9, before the new Congress, but Democrats' midterm wins create uncertainty: the bill was expected to pass with mostly Republican votes plus a few Democrats, and Democrats could instead wait until they control both chambers next year, though any deal still needs Trump's signature.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Lame-duck timing is a binary catalyst for permitting-sensitive energy and infrastructure names.
insights.locator: This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote

insights.claim: The American Clean Power Association largely supports BAAJA, with its analysis finding the bill could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Industry sees a large backlog of renewable capacity gated by permitting.

insights.claim: The Natural Resources Defense Council judges BAAJA's transmission provisions potentially very beneficial for the grid but warns that narrowing environmental reviews could damage public and private lands.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Environmental-group opposition signals litigation and amendment risk around review-narrowing provisions.

insights.claim: Rhodium Group's best case finds BAAJA would cut US economy-wide emissions 4%, lower annual household energy bills by $78, and add 200 GW of new clean energy by 2040, while its worst case leaves emissions roughly unchanged.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Quantifies upside for clean-energy capacity additions and a modest consumer-bill effect.
insights.locator: One, from the think tank Rhodium

insights.claim: Resources for the Future estimates BAAJA could cut US power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion in system costs by midcentury.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Large system-cost savings imply lower long-run power prices and grid investment efficiency.
insights.locator: Another report, from the nonprofit research

insights.claim: Purdue energy modeler Kevin Kircher found that had BAAJA been in force in 2025, US energy-sector emissions and air-pollution health risks would have been higher than the actual baseline, because easier permitting also expands fossil-fuel buildout.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Counters the consensus that permitting reform is net-green; gas infrastructure may be the larger beneficiary.
insights.quote: You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other

themes.theme: Data centers, gas and demand rebound

insights.claim: Data-center pressure on the US grid has triggered a wave of announced natural-gas plants, raising concern that BAAJA's main real-world effect would be to open the floodgates for new gas generation.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Permitting reform could accelerate gas-turbine and pipeline demand tied to AI load growth.

insights.claim: Easier permitting would yield more clean energy and more natural gas, and lower electricity prices could in turn raise demand and total emissions, so the emissions outcome depends on what actually gets built.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Investors should expect broad-based capacity growth rather than a clean-only buildout.
insights.quote: But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.

insights.claim: Climate advocates argue permitting reform favors renewables because solar and wind are among the cheapest power sources, so removing build constraints should let them win economically.

insights.so_what: Cost-competitiveness thesis underpins renewable developers' support for the bill.
